Olfaction: Basics and Odorants

Smell is a chemical sense, so its receptors are chemoreceptors.

In humans it is not necessary for survival, but it improves the quality of life, and it is more highly developed in females.

Significance of smell

  • Relation to taste: in severe rhinitis many foods lose their taste.
  • Effect on other organs: it may increase or decrease GIT secretion.
  • Psychogenic effect: pleasure with pleasant odors such as perfumes.
  • Protective function: dangerous odors (gases or fire) alarm us.

Requirements of an odorant substance

Volatile
To come in contact with the olfactory epithelium
Water soluble
To dissolve in the thin mucous layer over the receptors
Lipid soluble
To cross the cell membrane
Threshold concentration
Varies greatly from one substance to another

Remarks about olfaction

  • Sniffing deflects air upwards and increases sensitivity to odorous substances.
  • A change of more than 30% in concentration is needed for the receptors to differentiate it.
  • Continuous exposure to the same odor causes rapid adaptation (olfactory receptors are moderately adapting).
  • Heating a substance increases its ability to stimulate smell, because more volatile molecules are produced.
  • Individual sensitivity varies greatly: about 1000 different odorant receptors are encoded by about 1000 different genes.
  • Olfactory mucus contains odorant binding proteins that concentrate the odorants and transfer them to the receptors.

Olfactory Receptor Stimulation and Theories

The resting membrane potential of olfactory receptors is about -55 mV, with continuous discharge at 1 to 3 impulses per second. An odorant lowers the potential from -55 to -30 mV, raising the discharge up to about 20 impulses per second. A few odors instead hyperpolarize the receptors, decreasing discharge below the basal level.

Olfactory transduction

Transduction is the conversion of a chemical signal into an electrical signal that can be transmitted to the CNS.

  1. Odorant binding

    The odorant binds specific olfactory receptor proteins on the cilia of the receptor cells.

  2. G protein coupling

    The receptor proteins are coupled to adenylyl cyclase through a G protein, which is activated on binding.

  3. Adenylyl cyclase activation

    It converts ATP to cAMP, raising intracellular cAMP.

  4. Na+ channels open

    The rise in cAMP opens Na+ channels in the receptor cell membrane.

  5. Depolarization

    The depolarizing receptor potential brings the membrane closer to threshold and depolarizes the initial segment of the olfactory nerve axon.

  6. Action potentials

    They are generated and propagated along the olfactory nerve axons toward the olfactory bulb.

Theories of olfaction

Chemical theory

  • The transduction mechanism described above.

Physical theory

  • About 100 types of receptor sites for different odors on the receptor cell membrane.
  • Each odor joins one or more sites according to its molecular shape, and this binding stimulates the receptor.
  • Substances with different chemical properties but identical molecular shape have the same odor.

Olfactory Pathway

High-yield

Olfaction is the only sense with no area in the neocortex. It is detected mainly in the limbic system (old visceral cortex), and it is the only sensory pathway that does not relay in the thalamus.

Receptor cells
Olfactory nerve (CN I)
Glomeruli
Mitral and tufted cells
Olfactory tract
Three striae

First and second order neurons

  • First order neurons: the receptor cells in the olfactory mucosa. Their axons unite to form the olfactory nerve, which penetrates the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to enter the olfactory bulb.
  • Second order neurons: the mitral and tufted cells in the olfactory bulb. They synapse with axons of olfactory cells to form the olfactory glomeruli.

Other cells of the olfactory bulb

Periglomerular cells

  • Inhibitory neurons.
  • Connect one glomerulus to another.

Granule cells

  • Have no axons.
  • Make reciprocal synapses with the lateral dendrites of mitral and tufted cells.
  • Mitral or tufted cell excites the granule cell by glutamate; the granule cell inhibits it by GABA.

The glomeruli show lateral inhibition, mediated by periglomerular and granule cells, which sharpens and focuses olfactory signals. Different glomeruli are believed to respond to different odors.

Olfactory tract and striae

The axons of tufted and mitral cells pass posteriorly to form the olfactory tract, which enters the brain at the junction between the mesencephalon and the cerebrum and then divides into three striae.

StriaCourse / terminationFunction / note
MedialCrosses to the opposite side in the anterior commissureLesion causes marked decrease in olfactory sensation
LateralPrepyriform and pyriform cortex and amygdaloid nucleiVery old olfactory system; basic olfactory reflexes and learning to like or dislike some foods through experience
IntermediateOlfactory tubercle (in the anterior perforated substance) and nuclei anterior to the hypothalamusPrimitive responses to smell such as licking the lips and salivation
Newer pathway

A newer pathway passes through the dorsomedial thalamic nucleus to reach the orbitofrontal cortex, and is concerned with conscious analysis of different odors.

Taste: Importance and Receptors

Importance of taste

  • First line of defense against toxic, putrefied or undesirable food.
  • Evokes reflex stimulation of gastrointestinal secretions and motility.
  • Causes psychic happiness with pleasant tasty food.
  • Plays a role in homeostasis in some animals and, to a lesser extent, man: diabetic patients who lose much glucose in urine seek sugary food, while patients with Addison's disease prefer salty foods because of excessive NaCl loss in urine.

Taste receptors

Taste buds are chemoreceptors stimulated by food or other substances dissolved in the saliva of the buccal cavity.

  • Concentrated mainly on the dorsum and sides of the tongue.
  • The lower surface of the tongue, mucosa of the cheeks, lips and rest of the buccal cavity are nearly devoid of taste buds.
  • Scattered taste buds are present in the soft and hard palate, epiglottis and pharynx.
  • In infants and young children they occupy a larger area (the whole dorsum and even the buccal mucosa) and progressively decrease with advancing age.
  • Tongue mucosa is continually shed and regenerated, but taste receptors do not undergo such variation as readily.

Primary Taste Modalities

Humans can differentiate more than 200 taste sensations, yet there are five basic modalities. Any other taste is a mixture of different degrees of these five.

ModalityStimulusBetter felt at
SweetOrganic sugars (glucose, sucrose, fructose); saccharine; thaumatinTip of the tongue
SaltyIonized substances, e.g. NaClAnterior part of the dorsum
SourVinegar, citrus fruit (citric acid), sour milk (lactic acid)Edges of the tongue
BitterCaffeine, quinine, nicotine, strychnineBack of the dorsum
Umami (meaty)Amino acids, glutamate, particularly monosodium glutamateDorsum of the tongue
  • Saccharine: a synthetic material, 700 times more potent than sucrose; non-calorie, so useful for obese or diabetic patients.
  • Thaumatin: a protein isolated from African berries, 100,000 times as sweet as sucrose.
  • All five modalities are sensed on the pharynx and epiglottis.
  • The substance tested must reach a threshold concentration; in old people it must be higher because of atrophy of many taste buds.
  • Smell and heat greatly increase taste sensation.
  • Some substances injected intravenously can evoke taste, e.g. sodium dihydrochloride gives an intense bitter sensation.
  • High blood levels of bile in jaundice and of ketone bodies in diabetes can change sensitivity to these substances when applied topically to the tongue.
Clinical relevance

Electric current applied to the tongue evokes taste sensation, which is of great clinical value in locating a facial nerve lesion.

Mechanism of Taste Receptor Stimulation

Stimulation of the exposed microvilli at the taste pores by the dissolved substance evokes a generator potential in the receptor cells, which is transformed into an action potential in the nerve terminals. A protein secreted by Ebner's glands on the dorsum of the tongue binds, concentrates and transmits taste-producing substances to the receptor cells.

Sour
Activation of H+ gated cation channels, leading to blockage of K+ channels
Salty
Na+ influx through passive ungated channels
Sweet
Increase in intracellular cAMP, which reduces K+ conductance
Bitter
α-gustducin (G protein) decreases intracellular cAMP; some believe phospholipase C raises intracellular Ca2+
Umami
Activation of metabotropic and ionotropic glutamate receptors
  • Most taste buds contain receptors for more than one modality, with predominance of one.
  • Water is thought to stimulate taste receptors by washing certain ions from them, causing their discharge; it must flow over the tongue to be detected.

Taste Pathway

Taste buds

First order neurons

RegionNerveCell bodiesEnds in nucleus solitarius
Anterior two thirds of tongueChorda tympani (facial)Geniculate gangliaUpper part
Posterior third of tongueGlossopharyngealPetrosal gangliaMiddle part
Other sitesVagusNodose gangliaLower part

Second and third order neurons

  • Second order: axons from the nucleus solitarius ascend in the ipsilateral medial lemniscus and end in the posterior ventral nucleus of the thalamus.
  • Third order: axons run in the sensory radiation to the anterior insula and frontal operculum of the ipsilateral cortex, rostral to the face area of the postcentral gyrus. There is no other cortical radiation of taste.
Don't confuse

Taste from the anterior two thirds travels in the chorda tympani, but general sensation (pain, touch, temperature) from the same area travels in the lingual nerve, a branch of the trigeminal. The glossopharyngeal nerve innervates the posterior third.

Key Terms

Check yourself

Which nerves carry taste from the anterior two thirds and from the posterior third of the tongue?

The chorda tympani (facial nerve) for the anterior two thirds, and the glossopharyngeal nerve for the posterior third.

Name the three olfactory striae.

Medial (crosses in the anterior commissure), lateral (prepyriform and pyriform cortex and amygdaloid nuclei) and intermediate (olfactory tubercle and nuclei anterior to the hypothalamus).

What happens at the reciprocal synapse between mitral or tufted cells and granule cells?

The mitral or tufted cell excites the granule cell by releasing glutamate, and the granule cell inhibits the mitral or tufted cell by releasing GABA.

Which five modalities are the primary tastes?

Sweet, sour, bitter, salt and umami (meaty).

Key Points / Quick Review

Olfaction basics

  • Chemical sense; odorants must be volatile, water soluble and lipid soluble.
  • More than 30% concentration change is needed for discrimination; moderately adapting.
  • About 1000 odorant receptors encoded by about 1000 genes.

Olfactory transduction

  • Odorant, then G protein, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, opening of Na+ channels, depolarization.
  • Resting potential about -55 mV, falling to -30 mV on stimulation.
  • Chemical theory versus physical theory (about 100 receptor site types, molecular shape).

Olfactory pathway

  • Receptor cells, CN I through the cribriform plate, glomeruli, mitral and tufted cells, olfactory tract, three striae.
  • No neocortical area and no thalamic relay in the classic pathway; newer pathway via the dorsomedial thalamic nucleus to the orbitofrontal cortex.
  • Lateral inhibition by periglomerular and granule cells sharpens signals.

Taste receptors and modalities

  • Taste buds are mainly on the dorsum and sides of the tongue.
  • Five modalities: sweet (tip), salty (anterior dorsum), sour (edges), bitter (back), umami (dorsum).
  • Electric current on the tongue helps locate a facial nerve lesion.

Taste mechanisms

  • Sour: H+ gated channels and K+ channel blockage; salty: Na+ influx.
  • Sweet: cAMP rises; bitter: α-gustducin lowers cAMP; umami: glutamate receptors.

Taste pathway

  • CN VII (geniculate), CN IX (petrosal) and CN X (nodose) end in the upper, middle and lower nucleus solitarius.
  • Medial lemniscus, then posterior ventral thalamic nucleus, then anterior insula and frontal operculum.
